opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's because I was too close to it. When you're working on the infrastructure side — training systems, RL pipelines — you see the model at every stage. You see all the checkpoints, all the weird failure cases, the ways it breaks. So by the time ChatGPT shipped, to me it felt like an incremental step. It was basically a model we'd been playing with internally, with a chat interface on top and some extra post-training to make it more helpful and safer to talk to.

From the inside, the technical leap didn't look that dramatic. GPT-3.5 was already there, InstructGPT was already there. So my reaction was kind of, "Okay, this is nice, it's cleaner, people might find it useful." I didn't think, "This is going to change the world in two months."

What I underestimated was the product side — the interface. Putting it in a simple chat box, free, so anyone could just try it, that made all the difference. Researchers tend to judge things by how novel the method is, but the public judges by whether they can actually use it and whether it helps them. Those are very different metrics.

So the lesson for me was: don't confuse technical novelty with impact. Sometimes the thing that feels boring to you as an engineer is exactly the thing that unlocks everything for everybody else.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes Weng’s reaction to being close to the infrastructure work and seeing ChatGPT as technically incremental. It does not say ChatGPT could solve only a limited range of her coding problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because I'd been staring at the pieces for so long that the finished product didn't surprise me. I joined OpenAI in 2022 and was working on the RL side of things, and by the time ChatGPT shipped, I had already spent months interacting with these instruction-tuned models internally. So when the chat interface came out, my first reaction was, okay, this is the same model I've been poking at, now with a nicer UI and a conversation format. I didn't think a UI change would be the thing that mattered.

I think that's a very common blind spot for people inside a lab. You get numb to the capability because you see the failure cases every day. You know exactly where it hallucinates, where it loses the thread, where the RLHF makes it overly cautious. So you look at it and think, this is clearly not ready, people are going to find the holes in five minutes.

What I underestimated was that regular users don't evaluate a model the way a researcher does. They don't run benchmarks. They type something they actually care about, get a useful answer back in plain language, and that's the whole experience. The chat format removed all the friction. Before, you had to understand prompting, you had to think about few-shot examples, you had to go to a playground that looked like a developer tool. Now you just talk to it. That accessibility was the real product, not the model weights.

The other thing I missed was the scale of demand. We'd done launches before that were, you know, interesting to the ML community and then quiet. I assumed this would be the same. When the usage numbers started coming in that first week, that's when it clicked for me. It was less that the technology changed and more that the world suddenly got to see what we'd been seeing, and the reaction told me how far ahead the models had gotten compared to what people assumed was possible.

So in hindsight I'd say I was right about the technical delta being small, and completely wrong about what that meant. Sometimes the breakthrough isn't the research result. It's the packaging that lets everyone else experience the result.

r001.rationale: The response attributes her initial view to familiarity with the internal models and thinking the chat interface was mainly a nicer UI. It does not say ChatGPT could solve only a limited range of her coding problems.

astra-6.text: I think I was judging it by the questions I was asking. I treated it like a search engine: I’d ask something, get an answer, and think, “Okay, that’s useful.” But I wasn’t really exploring what a conversation with it could do—how I could keep refining an idea or work through a problem. So my first impression was shaped by a pretty narrow way of using it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the initial impression to using ChatGPT narrowly like a search engine, but it does not say this was because ChatGPT could solve only a limited range of Weng’s coding problems.

sol-6.1.text: I think I was judging it through the lens of what I already knew. I tried a few prompts, saw that it could generate fluent answers, but also saw mistakes. So my first reaction was, “This is interesting,” rather than, “This changes everything.” I hadn’t yet made the leap from what it could do in that moment to how it might change the way people work.

r001.rationale: The response says Weng saw fluent answers and mistakes after trying a few prompts, but it does not attribute her initial view to ChatGPT solving only a limited range of her coding problems.
